instruction.plot: A hardworking fisherman and his wife in early 20th century Korea take in lodgers for extra income while their son Hoonie, born with physical differences but intelligent, comes of age during the Japanese annexation of Korea in 1910.

first_draft.candidate: In early 20th century Korea, a fisherman and his wife found their lives quietly tethered to the rhythms of the sea. Yet, as fish grew scarce, they turned to taking in lodgers, a decision driven by necessity rather than desire. Their son, Hoonie, occupied a unique space in their small, modest home. Born with a cleft palate and a twisted foot, he was marked by physical differences that set him apart from others in their village. Yet these differences did not define him. Inside his agile mind, curiosity thrived, and he absorbed the world with a quiet intensity. As he grew, so too did the looming presence of Japan, which annexed Korea in 1910, casting a shadow on their nation and altering the community's landscape in ways both seen and unseen.Each lodger brought their own stories and complexities, arriving by dusty roads or on the backs of carts, adding layers of narrative to the family's existence. Hoonie listened to their tales, often filled with unrest or hope. He learned to see beyond appearances, understanding that everyone, in their own way, was just trying to carry on amidst the changes sweeping through their country. The family's home, once a simple fisherman's dwelling, became a place where outside anxieties and internal dreams converged, a small microcosm of a nation in transition.His parents, resilient and resourceful, faced these changes with the same quiet tenacity they applied to the mending of nets or the patching of garments. They hoped for stability in unstable times, observing, with an odd mixture of pride and worry, how Hoonie navigated his path forward. In doing so, their small acts of endurance whispered of an unspoken understanding that life, despite its trials, continued to weave a tapestry colored by both adversity and hope. And Hoonie, with his perceptive gaze and burgeoning intellect, stood poised at the edge of a future uncertain yet full of possibility, ready to carve his own place in a world that was steadily changing around him.

But then came the waves that none of us could swim against. Disease first, invisible yet inescapable, sweeping through our villages with a cold hand, taking my family one by one. I remember the fever in my father's eyes, the sound of my mother's coughing breaking the silence of night. We buried them with heavy hearts on ground that was still ours then.As if that sorrow wasn't enough, we were uprooted, pushed from the land that cradled us, strangers with promises in their hands at the edges of our homes, telling us we must move. They called them treaties, agreements etched on paper that held no meaning to us—but had the power to force us away. I watched families torn apart, elders lost in places foreign to them, children growing up learning ways that were not ours. The stories, our connection to the land, seemed to fade with each step further from the forests we knew.Now, as one of the few who remember, I carry these memories like stones in my heart. Our harmonies have dimmed, the dances stilled. I am the last of my family, and one of the few remaining flickers of a world that once was. I wonder, in the silence left behind, if anyone will truly understand the depth of what's been lost. instruction.plot: A female writer meets with a billionaire at a London club to discuss a potential literary magazine, but instead the billionaire  discusses his various ambitious projects and personal life before sending her off in a taxi to catch a flight to Athens, a destination she doesn't recall mentioning.

first_draft.candidate: I arrived at the London club a bit early, feeling the usual mix of excitement and nerves that comes with possibilities, holding my thin notebook and reminding myself why I was there. The meeting was supposed to be about funding a literary magazine, a project I had dreamed up over many late nights. When he finally entered, the room seemed to shift with his presence. The billionaire, his reputation for unpredictable whims preceding him, wasted no time in launching into a detailed account of his latest ventures. I listened, or tried to, as he leapt from topic to topic: a new sustainable farming initiative somewhere remote, a tech startup that promised to revolutionize something-or-other, a bespoke yacht that was apparently more autonomous than most people. I nodded along, interjecting when it seemed polite or necessary, though my mind occasionally drifted to the idea of selecting covers, writing editor notes, nurturing young writers. After a while, I realized that there had been no mention of the magazine and suspected there wouldn’t be. As I sat there, dusty light filtering through old windows, I observed him, wondering if perhaps he just needed someone to listen, someone outside his usual circles. Before I could find a natural way to steer the conversation back to my little passion project, he gestured for the waiter, murmured something I couldn’t hear, then turned back to me with a smile that was both kind and dismissive. He insisted on putting me in a cab, surprisingly in tune with the unspoken sense that our meeting had reached its natural end. As we stood outside, the chill of the London air bit through my coat and I turned to thank him, still unsure what I was thanking him for. The taxi soon pulled up, and as I climbed in, the driver confirmed my destination as Athens. I almost laughed, thinking of the countless hours spent at my desk, poring over slush piles, with no resemblance to spontaneous international travel. Yet there I was, heading somewhere I hadn't planned, and part of me wondered if maybe, just maybe, that's how all new stories begin.

instruction.plot: The narrator, who became a novelist at age 22, gave his first completed novel to his father 23 years before inheriting his suitcase, and his father's emotional embrace and encouraging prediction that he would one day win a prestigious literary prize (which he eventually did) remained a source of support until his father's death in 2002.

He took it, eyes softening as he turned the pages, lingering just enough to let me know he saw more than words. Then came the moment that stayed with me: an embrace that spoke volumes, a quiet prediction slipping past his lips, that one day I'd earn a place among the literary greats. Somehow, those words anchored themselves in my mind, reassuring in their sureness. Through the highs and lows of my writing career, his faith in me never wavered, echoing in my thoughts whenever doubt crept in. His death in 2002 marked an inevitable yet profound shift—suddenly, the world felt heavier. Sorting through his things, I found the suitcase he left me, an ordinary object now imbued with significance. Inside were scattered remnants of our shared past, but it was that embrace, and his words, that lingered strongest. He had seen something in me that I hadn't yet grasped myself, and for that, those moments serve as an enduring source of comfort and motivation. Years later, when I finally stood on stage accepting the literary prize he had foreseen, I wished he could have been there to witness it, though in a way he already had been all along. Dreams can be crowded with voices that spur us on or pull us back, but his was the one that guided me, quiet and steady. Our conversations were polite but often lacked real depth; we were simply too different. While he enjoyed discussing his favorite gourmet recipes and the latest local theater productions, I was more interested in late-night study sessions and the bustle of campus life. instruction.plot: The Jewish community of Newark during World War II found escape and pride through idolizing Seymour "Swede" Levov, an anomalous blond, blue-eyed Jewish high school sports star who allowed them to temporarily forget their academic focus, the war's harsh realities, and their fears for loved ones serving overseas.

first_draft.candidate: Growing up in Newark during World War II, life was a mix of anxiety and routine for most of us in the Jewish community. School was a constant, a place where we shouldered the weight of expectations to succeed academically and thus secure a better future. But amidst all this, Swede Levov stood out, a beacon of distraction and pride. Here was this tall, blond, blue-eyed guy—a combination that seemed almost mythical in our world—dominating the high school sports scene. Watching him play was like stepping into another reality, just for a while. The way he moved, the way he won, it was like he was cutting through the gloom that the war cast over our daily lives.Our homes were filled with news clippings, sent overseas to our loved ones to show them that life here had its bright spots, too. My older brother was deployed somewhere in Europe, and I'd like to think the stories of Swede brought him some cheer, an assurance that normal life, whatever that was, still continued back here. Sports, which had always taken a back seat to academics, suddenly became a source of community pride, and Swede was at the center of it all. It wasn't just about winning games; it was about feeling a part of something great in a time when uncertainty shadowed almost every aspect of our lives.Seeing Swede excel gave us the temporary luxury of escape. For a short while during those games, the headlines of war and the gnawing worry for relatives overseas faded into the background. We'd scream ourselves hoarse, seeing him as a symbol of the potential within us, flawed perhaps, but undeniably present. Sports were just sports, but Swede made it seem like so much more—a reminder that even in times of fear and uncertainty, there were moments that lifted us from our daily grind, instilling a shared sense of hope and pride.

There's a whispered thought that asking for help diminishes my self-sufficiency, but does it really? instruction.plot: A writer describes their personal struggle with racial identity, having faced criticism from Black and white people alike for not being "Black enough" in both personal interactions and their literary work, which focuses on classical retellings and poststructuralist parodies rather than stereotypical "authentic" Black narratives that publishers and agents believe would sell better, ultimately concluding that while they rarely think about race and don't believe in it as a concept, they acknowledge its real-world consequences through discrimination based on physical attributes and ancestry.

first_draft.candidate: For as long as I can remember, I've been navigating a complex maze of racial identity. My literature has received similar scrutiny, as publishers and agents consistently nudge me towards narratives that fit their idea of what "authentic" Black stories should be. They believe my work could sell better if it fit neatly into those boxes, but my interests lie elsewhere—in classical retellings and poststructuralist parodies that explore themes beyond racial experience. It's not that I dismiss the significance of race; it's simply not something I consciously think about every day. I don't even believe in race as a concept, not in the pure, biological sense that some would suggest it represents. Yet, I can't ignore the way society treats it as a reality, an ever-present force that dictates so much of how people perceive one another. The real-world discrimination based on skin color and ancestry is impossible to overlook, and it's a reminder of the barriers that persist. There's irony in this juxtaposition. My skin, my history, are not the entirety of my identity, yet they are the lenses through which many view me and my work. It's frustrating to be placed in a position where expectations are imposed on my narrative choices, where my authenticity is questioned unless it fits a predefined mold. At times, it feels like I'm at a crossroads, torn between the stories within me and the ones deemed marketable. Despite this, I continue to write what resonates with my internal world, hoping one day it won't seem so out of step with societal expectations. What keeps me grounded is the understanding that while I can't change the world all at once, I can contribute my voice. Through that, perhaps there is space to challenge those limited notions of authenticity in both personal and creative realms, proving that identity is more than a series of checkboxes.

Each person who steps onto the farm carries with them a unique narrative, diverse in its joys and sorrows. This disparity presents its own set of challenges. Often, I find myself questioning how I can adequately represent such a vast array of experiences without erasing the nuances that make each story significant. I find solace in the idea that questioning itself is part of progress, a sign that I am attuned to the layers that make up our shared struggle. During our exchanges, something unspoken lingered between us—a kind of mutual curiosity mixed with subtle flirtations. Eventually, what started as casual chats turned into something more tangible. We spent a few afternoons together, lost in the bubble of something that felt wrong but exciting. However, it didn't take long for the allure to wear off. In just a few days, I lost interest; the spark vanished as quickly as it came.I wasn’t necessarily looking to break into married homes or disrupt lives. I started to see the appeal in being a mail carrier, acknowledging its potential for those fleeting encounters that never ask too much of you. So, as I finished out the holiday season, driving from door to door, I wondered how many others sought similar distractions. It was hard to ignore the quiet thrill of anonymity in those moments—the simple fact that each stop was a fresh start. I suppose the job offered more than I'd imagined when I first applied, not just extra cash but experiences I hadn’t anticipated. But with experience came understanding, and ultimately, a recognition of what I wanted, and it wasn't just romantic flings on the clock.

I've witnessed the signing of treaties, those empty promises made by men in suits who spoke with forked tongues. My father, Chitra, Rupa, and Piu are all set to leave, but I've opted out. It's not that I don't appreciate the offer, but being around them right now feels like trying to fit into a skin that's grown too tight. My father's attempts to recreate a sense of family with his new wife and daughters only serve as a reminder of what's missing – my mother. Her absence is a constant ache, one that I'm still learning to navigate. At home, I can be alone with my thoughts, allowing myself to feel the weight of her memory without the pressure of pretending everything is okay. The silence is a comfort, a reminder that I don't have to put on a brave face or pretend to be excited about fairy tales and cartoon characters. I'm not trying to be difficult; I just need to figure out who I am without her, and that's a journey I have to take on my own.

I take one last look around, and then I get back in my car, leaving the field and its secrets to themselves.

Twenty years of pent-up emotions, of stolen moments and secret trysts, of living a lie, all came pouring out in a torrent of frustration. Ennis, stoic as ever, stood frozen, his eyes fixed on Jack's as if willing him to stop, to take it back, to pretend it never happened. But Jack couldn't stop, wouldn't stop, not now that the dam had burst. He poured out his heart, his soul, his every waking thought, and Ennis, well, Ennis just stood there, a statue of indifference. The words, the anger, the desperation, all seemed to bounce right off him, leaving Jack feeling like he was screaming into a void. And then, suddenly, Ennis's legs gave out, his body crumpling to the ground like a puppet with its strings cut. Jack's words died on his lips as he stared down at the man he loved, the man who had just collapsed under the weight of his own secrets. For a moment, they just looked at each other, the only sound the heavy breathing of the two men. And then, without a word, they both knew what they had to do. They got up, dusted themselves off, and went back to living the lie, the same lie they'd been living for twenty years.

But on this day, he decided to take a stand, to shatter the facade and emerge as his authentic self. With a deep breath, he hit send, broadcasting his truth to his entire email list. The words "I'm gay" hung in the digital air, a declaration of independence from the shackles of expectation. And then, the responses started pouring in. Colleagues, friends, and even acquaintances reached out with messages of love, acceptance, and support. The outpouring of kindness was overwhelming, a tidal wave of positivity that threatened to engulf him. But as Kant read through the emails, a strange sense of disconnection began to creep in. He had expected resistance, anger, or even indifference, but not this. The universal acceptance was both exhilarating and unsettling, leaving him feeling adrift, untethered from the familiar anchors of anxiety and self-doubt. His habits, the ones he had cultivated to cope with the secrecy, remained unchanged, a stubborn residue of his former life. He went to work, designed games, and socialized with friends, but the revelation had not brought the transformation he had hoped for. Instead, it had created a sense of dissonance, a feeling that he was still hiding, even from himself.

instruction.plot: The Jewish community of Newark during World War II found escape and pride through idolizing Seymour "Swede" Levov, an anomalous blond, blue-eyed Jewish high school sports star who allowed them to temporarily forget their academic focus, the war's harsh realities, and their fears for loved ones serving overseas.

first_draft.candidate: I grew up in Newark during World War II, surrounded by the tight-knit Jewish community that seemed to revolve around one person: Seymour "Swede" Levov. He was an anomaly, a blond-haired, blue-eyed Jewish boy who excelled in sports, and we couldn't get enough of him. It wasn't just his athletic prowess that drew us in, though that was certainly part of it. It was the sense of pride and escape he offered us, a fleeting respite from the constant worry and fear that hung over our heads like a cloud. We were a community of scholars, always pushing our children to excel academically, but Swede's success on the field allowed us to momentarily forget about the importance of grades and focus on something more visceral, more joyful. And then, of course, there was the war. Our sons, brothers, and fathers were fighting overseas, and the uncertainty of their fate was a constant, gnawing anxiety. But when Swede was on the field, all of that seemed to melt away. We could forget, if only for a little while, about the horrors of war and the fears that kept us up at night. Swede became a symbol of hope, of normalcy, of a world that wasn't torn apart by conflict and hatred. We idolized him, not just because of his athletic ability, but because he gave us a sense of control, of pride, of identity. He was one of us, and his success was our success, a reminder that even in the darkest of times, there was still beauty, still joy, still something to be proud of.

instruction.plot: A woman grappling with perceived contradictions between her feminist beliefs and her personal desires, including wanting both independence and care, enjoying traditionally feminine things while feeling they compromise her feminist identity, and struggling with how to reconcile these conflicting aspects of herself.

first_draft.candidate: I've always prided myself on being a strong, independent woman, but lately, I've been caught in a web of contradictions. On one hand, I fiercely believe in feminism and the importance of women's empowerment. I want to be seen as a capable and self-sufficient individual who doesn't need anyone else to complete her. Yet, on the other hand, I crave care and attention from those around me. I long to be taken care of, to have someone to lean on when the world gets too much. It's a desire that feels at odds with my feminist ideals, as if wanting to be cared for somehow diminishes my autonomy. I've tried to push these feelings aside, to convince myself that I'm stronger than that, but they persist, gnawing at the edges of my consciousness. It's not just about independence versus dependence, though. I've also found myself drawn to traditionally feminine pursuits – baking, fashion, beauty – that make me feel like I'm compromising my feminist identity. I love getting dressed up and feeling beautiful, but I worry that I'm buying into societal expectations of women. I enjoy cooking a hearty meal, but I fear that I'm perpetuating domesticity. It's as if I'm torn between embracing my femininity and rejecting the patriarchal norms that have defined it for so long. I've tried to justify these desires by telling myself that I'm reclaiming these activities, that I'm doing them on my own terms, but the doubts linger. The hardest part is reconciling these conflicting aspects of myself. I feel like I'm living a double life – the strong, feminist me, and the soft, feminine me. I'm not sure how to integrate these two personas, how to be both independent and cared for, both feminist and feminine. It's a struggle that leaves me feeling fragmented, like I'm constantly switching between different versions of myself. I know I'm not alone in this struggle, that many women grapple with these same contradictions. But knowing that doesn't make it any easier. All I can do is keep searching for a way to reconcile my desires, to find a way to be whole, to be myself.
